references.text: In [ref:Joh 4:39-41|John 4:39-41], the preceding context is described: many Samaritans believed first because of the woman's testimony, but even more came to believe when they heard Jesus themselves. Verse 42 summarizes this by saying to the woman that they now believe because of their own encounter with Jesus.

In [ref:Joh 4:29|John 4:29], the woman asks if Jesus can be the Messiah. In verse 42, the confession goes further: the Samaritans confess him not only as the Messiah, but as the Savior of the world – a deeper recognition than the woman's original question.

John the Baptist testifies in [ref:Joh 1:29|John 1:29] that Jesus is "the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world". The expression "Savior of the world" in John 4:42 reflects this universal dimension of Jesus' work.

[ref:1 Joh 4:14|1 John 4:14] uses exactly the same expression: "The Father has sent the Son as the Savior of the world" (ὁ σωτὴρ τοῦ κόσμου). This is the only other occurrence of this expression in the New Testament.

In [ref:Joh 3:16-17|John 3:16-17], Jesus says that God sent his Son into the world to save the world, not to condemn it. The Samaritans' confession that Jesus is "the Savior of the world" confirms precisely this universal purpose of salvation.

In [ref:Jes 43:3|Isaiah 43:3], the Lord calls himself Israel's Savior. The confession of Jesus as "the Savior of the world" shows that the Old Testament title of Savior is now extended to include all peoples, including the Samaritans.

In [ref:Jes 49:6|Isaiah 49:6], the Lord says that his servant shall be a light for the nations and bring salvation to the ends of the earth. The Samaritans' confession of Jesus as the Savior of the world fulfills this prophecy of salvation extending beyond Israel's borders.

In [ref:Apg 4:12|Acts 4:12], Peter proclaims that there is no salvation in any other than Jesus. The Samaritans' confession of Jesus as the Savior of the world points to the same exclusive and universal truth of salvation.

In [ref:Joh 6:69|John 6:69], Peter confesses: "We believe and know that you are the Holy One of God". The Samaritans' "we know" (οἴδαμεν) in 4:42 reflects the same type of personal confession of faith based on their own experience with Jesus.
